paras: The lynching of three Black men near Lockesburg, Arkansas, took place in early June 1881, when armed white men in Sevier County hunted down three unnamed men accused of robbing and murdering a farmer, R. F. Hall, and hanged them from trees at a ford on Rolling Fork Creek. The first man, called the ringleader, was hanged on his capture, and the other two were reported hanged on the night of Tuesday, June 7. Dispatches from Little Rock carried the story nationally within days, several presenting the hangings as deserved retribution.

According to the Little Rock dispatches, Hall was an old farmer living near Lockesburg, also spelled Locksburg, who set out to visit friends or relatives in an adjoining county. Finding Rolling Fork Creek swollen by recent rains, he hired three Black men to help him across, and he was reputed to carry a large sum of money. The dispatches charged that the three knocked him down, took twenty-five or thirty cents from his pockets, strangled him, and weighted the body before throwing it into the creek. The body lodged in drift downstream, where, the Chicago Tribune's second dispatch said, a Black man saw and recognized it.

The discovery aroused the neighborhood, and the dispatch to the New Orleans Democrat said that "an old negro" gave a clue to the men, who had taken to the woods. The pursuers were called "a band of armed men", "a large body of white men", and in the Associated Press wire "a vigilance committee". The first man captured was taken back to the creek and hanged from the limb of a tree; the Tribune said he confessed and "begged piteously for life", while the Democrat's correspondent wrote that he admitted his part but said he had been drunk.

The other two were later found in the woods, or by another account overtaken "many miles from the scene", and were brought back to the ford, the scene of the alleged crime, and hanged from a tree near their companion. None of the men or their captors was named, and the confessions are reported only from the lynchers' side.

The Tribune's first dispatch reported "a whirlwind of excitement" in the vicinity and said the action of "Judge Lynch" was "universally approved", while the Democrat's version said "generally approved". No report of an inquest, arrest or other official response appears in the coverage.

The story first appeared on June 9 in a special dispatch to the Memphis Daily Appeal headed "Three Negro Murderers Lynched" and in the Chicago Tribune under "Speedy Justice". On June 10 the Tribune printed a fuller Little Rock dispatch as "Just Retribution", and the same text ran in the Gold Hill Daily News, the Cheyenne Daily Leader and, as "Judge Lynch", the Washington Standard. A shorter National Associated Press wire, printed in the Wheeling Daily Intelligencer and the Omaha Daily Bee, credited the hangings to a vigilance committee and said the men killed Hall "to prevent punishment for the assault". On June 13 the Savannah Morning News reprinted the Democrat's account under "Judge Lynch at Work".

Condensed versions ran in news summaries from Lancaster, Pennsylvania, to Sacramento, California, and in the Batesville Guard in Arkansas, calling the dead men "the murderers". The longer accounts called the accused "darkeys" and "guilty wretches" and presented the accusation as established fact. Weeks later, on July 24, the Seattle Daily Intelligencer retold the episode as a series of the accused men's mistakes, ending with mounted lynchers who "hanged them without trial".

Nearly every account gives three men lynched, but the Warren Sheaf said only "two of the murderers were captured and lynched". The Tribune's June 10 dispatch had the last two found before dark after a few hours' pursuit, while its June 9 dispatch and the Democrat's placed their capture on Tuesday night and their hanging by midnight or in the moonlight. The Seattle retelling instead had the pursuit last three days and put the sum taken at $1. The victim's name appears as R. F. Hall in the detailed dispatches but as "Hull" in the Watertown Republican and "A. F. Hall" in the Batesville Guard.

bases: Armed white men pursued three Black men accused of murdering R. F. Hall, brought them back to the ford and hanged them from trees, with no officers or trial reported (A1, A2, A6).

Three men (two in one brief) were hanged by 'a band of armed men', 'a large body of white men' or 'a vigilance committee' acting without any lawful authority or trial, as punishment for an accused murder (A2, A5, A6); the Seattle retelling says 'without trial' (A30).

Separate Little Rock dispatches to the Memphis Appeal, the Chicago Tribune, the National Associated Press and the New Orleans Democrat agree on the core event, though all derive from news reaching Little Rock and one brief gives two lynched rather than three (A1, A2, A5, A20, A24).

accounts.label: Chicago Tribune special, June 8
accounts.gist: A band of armed men hunted the three; the ringleader confessed, begged for life and was hanged at the creek; the other two were captured Tuesday at nightfall and hanged by midnight.

accounts.label: Little Rock wire of June 9-10 (Tribune 'Just Retribution')
accounts.gist: A large body of white men gathered at the ford; after a few hours one man was caught and hanged, and before dark the other two were found hiding in the woods, confessed, and were hanged beside him.

accounts.label: National Associated Press wire
accounts.gist: A vigilance committee lynched the three at Rolling Fork for murdering Hall, whom they killed after robbing him of a few cents 'to prevent punishment for the assault'.

accounts.label: Dispatch to the New Orleans Democrat
accounts.gist: An old Black man gave a clue; the ringleader admitted his part but said he was drunk and was hanged despite his pleas; the other two were overtaken Tuesday night many miles away and hanged by moonlight.

accounts.label: Seattle retelling
accounts.gist: The men found only $1 on the traveler; mounted lynchers pursued them three days and hanged them without trial.

framing.detail: The Chicago Tribune headed its dispatches 'Speedy Justice' and 'Just Retribution', called the accused 'darkeys' and 'guilty wretches', and said Judge Lynch's action was 'universally approved'.
The Savannah Morning News, reprinting the New Orleans Democrat, headed it 'Judge Lynch at Work' and spoke of 'swift retribution' that was 'generally approved'.
News summaries and roundups (Lancaster, Sacramento, Watertown, Batesville, Warren, Milan) gave one or two sentences calling the dead men 'the murderers' and saying they confessed.
The Seattle Daily Intelligencer told it as a string of the accused men's 'mistakes', ending flatly that lynchers 'hanged them without trial'.
